title: No frenzy, no pretense
hook: perfect character lives each day as the last, without frenzy, dullness or pretense (Meditations 7.69)

segments.voice: Yesterday: wrestling, not dancing, the art of staying steady when grabbed. Your line was a hand grabs his ankle. Today closes the week, and the book.

Tell people to live each day as if it were their last, and you get three kinds of reaction. One person books a skydiving trip and quits their job by noon. Another sighs and goes back to bed: what's the point. A third posts a beautiful quote about seizing the day, then spends the afternoon exactly as before. Near the end of book seven, Marcus Aurelius names all three, and rules out every one.
screen: `SKYDIVING BY NOON.` → `BACK TO BED.` → `A BEAUTIFUL QUOTE.`

segments.voice: Meditations seven, sixty-nine, in George Long's translation: "The perfection of moral character consists in this, in passing every day as the last, and in being neither violently excited nor torpid nor playing the hypocrite." One instruction, then three warnings. Violently excited is the skydiver: if today is the last, cram it full, grab everything. Marcus says no. A last day lived in a panic isn't lived well. Torpid means sluggish, numb: the one who goes back to bed. Thinking about death can make people give up, and Marcus rules that out too. Playing the hypocrite is the beautiful quote with no change behind it, wearing the costume of a serious life without living it. Remove all three, and what's left is calm, awake and real. That's the last day Marcus wants: unhurried, attentive and honest. Not dramatic at all. And it closes this week well: all will forget, kin, think of what you have, vine, mat, wrestling, not dancing, and this. Each is a way of living one ordinary day fully, without forcing it. Book seven ends soon after this entry, and tomorrow book eight begins.
screen: `EACH DAY AS THE LAST.` · `NOT VIOLENTLY EXCITED.` · `NOT TORPID.` · `NOT PLAYING THE HYPOCRITE.` · then, large: `NO FRENZY, NO PRETENSE.`

segments.voice: Imagine this really were your last day, and let the frenzy that wants to rise pass, then any heaviness, then any wish to look like you're doing this well. What's left is you, breathing, here, awake. Stay in that plain, unhurried attention.
No frenzy. Marcus's picture of a well-lived day, each as the last, without frenzy, dullness or pretense. Today's word.
Your line: quits their job by noon. Not frenzy, not dullness, not pretense: just the day, lived plainly. A week, and a book, complete.

howItsDone: Readers of Marcus often use 7.69 to check how they're living a day: not rushed and grasping, not numb, and not putting on a show of a meaningful life.

fork.setup: you take 'live each day as your last' to heart this morning. which way does Marcus mean it?

fork.reveal: Meditations 7.69: passing every day as the last, neither violently excited nor torpid nor playing the hypocrite.

trapdoor: what you thought: seize the day, grab every thrill.
what it means: a last day well lived is calm, awake and honest, not frantic, numb or performed.
what a scholar hears: the Greek for 'playing the hypocrite' comes from the word for a stage actor, hypokritēs, so Marcus is warning against acting out a good life.
recall: flattery of the powerful, out of fear
guess: living each day as the last, but calmly, without a rush
cramming every day full, since it could be your last
giving up on plans, since any day could be the end
